questions.stimulusText:
Some machines receive force in separate pushes rather than in a perfectly steady stream. Without a way to bridge the intervals, their speed would rise during each push and fall between pushes. A flywheel helps reduce this unevenness. It is a wheel designed to store energy while rotating.
When an input speeds the flywheel up, some of the supplied energy becomes stored rotational energy. Between inputs, the turning wheel can give up part of that reserve while helping the connected mechanism continue moving. Its speed decreases as it releases energy, but the variation can be smaller than it would be without the wheel.
How the mass is arranged matters. For the same total mass, placing more of it farther from the axle makes the wheel resist changes in rotational speed more strongly. This resistance does not mean the wheel can never speed up or slow down; it means changing its motion requires more energy transfer.
A flywheel is therefore a temporary store, not a source that produces energy by itself. Friction gradually takes energy from the moving system. If no new input arrives, the wheel eventually slows to a stop. A well-designed flywheel can smooth the delivery of energy, but it cannot remove the need to supply energy in the first place.

questions.prompt: In the imagined tradition, which event must every teller preserve?

choices.A: Every passenger eats an identical meal.
choices.B: A particular joke is repeated word for word.
choices.C: The fishing crew returns before a storm.
choices.D: The boat is described with the same adjectives.

questions.correctAnswer: The fishing crew returns before a storm.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph explicitly identifies the crew's return before the storm as part of the plot that every teller must preserve.
questions.stimulusText:
Readers can compare two copies of a printed story word for word. Differences may be treated as printing mistakes. That expectation is less useful for understanding an oral tradition in which each performance is allowed to vary. Consider the following imagined tradition, whose rules make this distinction clear.
Its central tale concerns a fishing crew that must return before a storm. That return is part of the plot every teller must preserve. Other features are open to invention. The meal on the boat, a passenger's description, or a joke told during the voyage can change for a particular audience. Such embellishment gives the teller room to make the performance immediate.
Listeners who know the tradition judge more than exact wording. They may welcome a new joke while objecting to a change that removes the crew's reason for hurrying. A transcript alone could show which words differ, but understanding those differences requires knowing what the tradition holds fixed and what it permits a teller to reshape.
The common plot is a spine, not a cage. It supports the tale without dictating every movement of its telling. This does not mean that any version is acceptable. It means that continuity can depend on preserving important relationships between events while allowing the language around them to remain alive.

questions.stimulusText:
In our fencing drill, the first light tap on a partner's padded vest counted as a touch. We called our own touches when nobody else could see them. My vest had remained untouched all afternoon, and I was beginning to enjoy the clean column beside my name.
Then Jalen stepped in. I felt a small tap below my shoulder just before my own blade reached his vest. My arm had hidden the moment from the coach. Jalen lowered his blade and waited.
"Yours?" the coach asked me.
I could have nodded. It would have been a tiny movement, easier than explaining the sequence. Jalen was already looking toward the next pair, giving me no accusing stare to resist.
The coach's pencil hovered above the page. I looked at the empty column, then at the faint mark on my vest. I could not make what I had felt disappear simply by choosing a different answer.
"His first," I said.
The pencil moved. Jalen raised his blade again and gave me the same quick nod he had given before every other exchange. Nothing in his manner announced that I had done something remarkable.
I pulled my mask back into place. It had not lost any metal, but it sat more lightly on my head.

The apple contains enzymes, proteins that help particular reactions occur, as well as compounds those enzymes can act on.

Materials that were separated can now meet, and oxygen can participate in the reactions that lead to brown pigments. The visible color therefore reflects several requirements coming together.
Different conditions can affect different requirements. A coating that limits oxygen reaching the surface acts as a barrier. It need not remove the enzymes to reduce the reaction. These approaches act in different ways rather than making every part of the process disappear.

questions.stimulusTitle: The Cost of an Empty Seat
questions.stimulusText:
Consider a simplified ferry service with one sailing already scheduled. For that sailing, the crew receives the same pay and the dock charges the same fee whether the boat carries many passengers or few. These are fixed costs for this decision. Printing an additional ticket, by contrast, adds a small cost when another passenger boards; that is a variable cost.
An empty seat does not make the crew's pay disappear. When fewer passengers buy tickets, the fixed costs are spread among fewer people. The average cost per passenger can therefore rise even if the total cost of the sailing changes very little.
Average cost is not the same as the extra cost of serving one more passenger. Suppose the scheduled sailing is currently losing money. An additional fare could exceed the extra ticket-printing cost without covering a full share of the crew's pay. The difference would contribute toward fixed costs, though the sailing might remain unprofitable.
The decision's boundary matters. Operating a second boat requires another crew and another dock fee in this model. A cost fixed while filling an existing boat can increase when another sailing is added. Calling a cost fixed is therefore useful only after the decision has been defined; it does not mean that the cost can never change.

The tapping began after my cousin Aven fell asleep. Three quick knocks, a pause, then two more. Beyond the tent wall, the darkness seemed to be waiting for me to answer.
I had insisted on taking the side nearest the entrance. Earlier, that had meant an easy way out to watch the sunset. Now it meant being closest to whatever had found us.
The knocks stopped. I held my breath. When they began again, they sounded lower down, near the opening where my boots stood. I lifted the lantern but kept its light pointed at my blanket, as though the brightness might announce where I was.
Aven stirred. "Wind," she murmured, and turned over.

I tucked the pull into the boot and moved the flask. The next gust made only a soft flutter.

questions.stimulusText:
A bar magnet has a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other. The names describe magnetic behavior: like poles repel, while unlike poles attract. Cutting the bar between its ends might seem to offer a way to obtain a north-only piece and a south-only piece. That is not what happens. Each piece has both a north pole and a south pole.
A useful model looks inside the material. In an iron magnet, tiny regions called domains behave like small magnets. Within a domain, magnetic effects point in a common direction. When many domains are aligned, their effects reinforce one another and produce the magnet's larger overall effect.
Cutting the bar divides the material, but it does not sort north poles into one pile and south poles into another. In the simplified model, the aligned regions remaining in each piece still produce a magnet with two poles. If the pieces stay in their original orientation, the newly exposed faces have opposite poles and attract one another.
The model also distinguishes a region's behavior from the whole object's behavior. In an unmagnetized piece of iron, domains can point in different directions, largely canceling their effects. A weak overall effect therefore need not mean that the small regions themselves have stopped behaving magnetically.

questions.stimulusTitle: Two Shapes in a Soap Film
questions.stimulusText:
A soap film stretched across a flat wire loop can look nearly flat, while a free-floating soap bubble is usually round. The contrast does not mean that the liquid follows two unrelated principles. Its shape depends on both a common tendency and the restrictions placed on it.
Surface tension makes a liquid surface behave somewhat like a stretched skin. Reducing surface area reduces the energy associated with that surface. A film therefore tends toward a smaller area, but it cannot ignore the boundaries or enclosed space involved in a particular situation.
On a flat wire loop, the rim fixes the film's edge. A nearly flat sheet can span the opening bounded by that rim with little area. A bubble, however, encloses air. In an ideal comparison between shapes enclosing the same volume, a sphere uses the least surface area. The round shape follows from minimizing area while preserving an enclosed volume, not from a rule requiring every film to become a sphere.
Real shapes can be affected by air currents, gravity, or contact with other bubbles. Such complications do not make the simple comparison useless. It identifies which restriction matters: the fixed rim for the flat film and the enclosed volume for the bubble. Asking only whether the material is soapy misses the conditions that help determine its form.
